d: Loss of ovarian follicle function before age 40, shown by amenorrhea with an FSH in the menopausal range on two occasions. Causes include fragile X premutation, autoimmunity, Turner mosaicism and chemotherapy.
Amenorrhea from slowed GnRH pulses caused by low energy availability, intense exercise or stress. FSH, LH and estradiol are low, and bone loss is a risk.
The liver protein that binds testosterone and estradiol in blood. Insulin lowers its production, so insulin resistance raises the free, active fraction of testosterone.

The PCOS definition: two of oligo- or anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia and nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

A memory scheme for abnormal uterine bleeding. Structural causes are polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma and malignancy or hyperplasia. Nonstructural causes are coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic and not otherwise classified.
An x-ray study in which contrast is pushed through the cervix to outline the uterine cavity and tubes. Free spill into the peritoneum shows the tubes are open.

A scheme that sorts amenorrhea by the failing level: I the uterus and outflow tract, II the ovary, III the anterior pituitary, IV the hypothalamus. Failure of II is hypergonadotropic, and III or IV is hypogonadotropic.

Menstrual blood trapped in the vagina behind an imperforate hymen or transverse vaginal septum. It presents at puberty with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, a bulging bluish membrane and a lower-abdominal mass.

An in vitro fertilization step in which a single sperm is injected directly into each egg. It treats severe male-factor infertility and is paired with surgical sperm retrieval when the ejaculate has no sperm.
